projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Frank D. Buehl was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Which branch of the service did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Air Force...

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What day were you honorably discharged?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I joined in March of 1942. Let's see, I was not discharged; I was separated from active duty in January of 1960. Wait a minute let me correct that not 1960, 1953, not 1960.1 was separated from the service in January of 1953.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What was the highest rank you ever achieved?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Captain.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Where were you living at the time of enlistment?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Memphis.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I wanted to be a flyer. Pilot.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Why did you pick the service that you joined?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: To learn how to fly.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What did you feel like when you first got there?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well we didn't call it boot camp, I think that's the Navy or Marine version but uh it was tough at times hazing was going on at that point. However I made it.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you remember your drill instructors at all?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: How did you get through it?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: How'd I get through it? Ok.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Where exactly did you go when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: To start with? Oh lord(laughs) I went all around the world. I cant think of all of them but I started out at Maxwell Field, Alabama. Montgomery, Alabama I ended up in Japan and places in between.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you remember arriving at the first place overseas and do you remember what it was like?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: First place overseas, I was in Libya, Benghazi, Libya. I was a pilot of a bomber crew then and we flew from Kansas all the way to England, then to Libya, that took quite a while back then.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What was your exact job that you had to do?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I was a pilot of a four engine bomber.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you ever see combat?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Yes Were there any casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Yes, now you said unit that covers a lot of ground, and (camera man speaks) well let me go a little different from that. I was a pilot of a crew of 10 men, my bomb group was early in the war, we were bombing in Europe and as how many were killed there's no way to asses that situation. I lost..., I lost three men in my own crew, uh I could go on and on about this, but you go ahead.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Tell me about a few of your most memorable experiences.

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well getting shot down over enemy territory and having to parachute out of a burning airplane that was sort of memorable. You'd like to know about that? Well I... we were shot down over Greece, Athens, which was enemy territory at that time, and we were bombing an airport at Athens where the Germans were operating. And an old lumbering four engine plane is no match for a bunch of German fighters. Out of 18 planes they shot down 3 of them, some of my crew and some from another crew were captured by the Germans. But uh 5 out of my crew we landed on top of a mountain in Greece, and the reason that was a safe place to be is because the Germans were in the valleys in the country, so to make a long story short we escaped from Greece after 19 days. Now I could get into how all that happened but I don't want to get into that now, that... I'd take up to much of your time. When we get finished here I, see some of this stuff here your welcome to read this to find out what happened to me and my cohorts. Now you want to go on?

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you still have your medals?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: There up in the attic, well the purple heart medal, air medal with oak leaf cluster, then several theatre of operation ribbons and medals. I cant think of the name of them right at this point, but I think I have about 8 of them up there.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: How did you attain them?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well, military merit and flying so many bombing missions and so fourth. And uh, now were talking about World War II now, I was also in the Korean war now that's another story. So I'm only talking about World War II at this point. And uh, I was actually after World War II I was a commissioned officer, and you're either on active duty or inactive duty. After World War II... was over, I went to inactive duty and I stayed in inactive duty, in a reserve unit, and I was here in Memphis, and when the Korean War came along I was activated again, back to active duty. And I said I was in Japan flying troop carriers not bombers, I didn't get shot at in that war. So it wasn't so bad but that from the day I first enlisted in the military, till I got out was roughly a 10 year span.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family during the wars?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well that was difficult back in World War II days and the Korean war, when I watch television now a days and see men in combat over in Iraq communicating with their families back here just blows my mind, because the only way we had of communicating was writing a letter and even that didn't work very well, as a matter of fact when I left this country in World War II I didn't hear from anybody or anything until I was I ended up in a hospital in Cario, Egypt. After this experience I told you about that's when I got my first mail from home that was about a 2 or 3 month period. So communication was not very well back then, it was practically nil, nobody knew where nobody was back then.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No the food was not good in Africa which is where Libya is when we went on bombing missions we were given k rations which is food in a box dried up food and so forth, and well I don't know about that's big *hand signs* any GI from World War II knows about K rations they were just rations, that was it but no food was not good then, my base in Africa was in the desert we lived in tents, living quarters were bad that was in World War II but it wasn't as bad as some people had it, on the ground all the time but no food was not good.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies, did you ever have supply problems?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well all my supplies was a parachute just that but now I'm talking about food in World War II, now back in the states and Japan and Korea the food was not bad, so that parts all right.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you ever feel any pressure or stress?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: An what, yeah I think I did on this bombing mission I was telling you about our plane was on fire and three engines were not running so my job as a pilot was to keep the plane so that everybody could get out of it! And yeah that's quite stressful if you have ever jumped out of an airplane before which is out of control and on fire it a little stress there. So im lucky to be here.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Was there ever a ritual or a ceremony that you did for luck?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: For luck? No.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: How did the pilots and crews entertain themselves during their off time?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well, I'm talking mainly about World War II there really was no off time so to speak, you're living in a tent in the desert not living close to anything so we really did not have any off time back then, you may be referring to a furlough which before a person would go into combat they were given a week or so off, but what did I do back then I was married back then, so I tried to see my wife that's the extent of that, but the guys they played cards, shoot craps something like that not much.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Was entertainment ever brought to the bases?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No, not where I was.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What did you do when you were on leave?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I'd come home from wherever I was and that's about the extent of it.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Where did you travel while in the service?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I was in England, North Africa which covers Algiers, Tunis, Cairo, then I visited Greece when I wasn't on leave or anything that was a little different. Then I was coming home from Africa spent some time in South America and Puerto Rico, and the Koran war spent time in Japan and Korea.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you recall any funny or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No, things were not really funny back then really no I cant.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Were pranks ever played?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No not really.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What did you think of officers and other fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well I was an officer myself, so I thought it was pretty good people, all of the men I knew were officers or what I got along with we were all in the same boat, so we got along.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you ever keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you have any photographs?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: In January of 1953 and no I don't recall the date.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Can you tell me about it?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well I was actually was in Atlanta, GA, was where I got out of the service completely.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: What did you do in the days and the week after you were discharged?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well now lemme back up I was in Atlanta, GA when I got out of service completely that was during the Korean war, well now you asked me what did I do when I was separated from active duty in World War II I went to work as an airline pilot in Kansas city Missouri, I also did after airline flying I moved back to Memphis and I worked for ford motor company in the sales dept, from there I went on back to active duty when I got back went to work for Ford Motor Company, I left Ford Motor Company and I spent 40 years in the lumber business here in Memphis, that ended about 12 years ago, now I don't do anything but play golf, do you want me to get on another subject I don't wanna get off to another subject, but my wife passed away last December so that makes a different life I live here alone, I not re-married or anything it's a lonesome life but I put up with it.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: 0h yeah very much so and you're going to ask me if some of them are still living? Well there's one friend that's still living he lives in Birmingham, Alabama, he's a little bit older than I am. Those pictures up there show some of my friends who passed away who I was very close to but yes I do have a few around, you know my friends that I'm speaking of and myself are members of Tom Brokaw's Greatest Generation, you know what that is there are not many of us left now. I'm 84 years old and I'm in good health. I have lost a lot of friends they just got to old, I think that's one of the questions on down the line.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: For how long have you been friends with these people?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: The one that's still living 60-65 years.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did you ever join any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I belong to my old bomb group association.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Can you tell me about your family?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: I have two daughters, my oldest daughter lives in Oregon and is 60 years old now, my youngest daughter a teacher she lives in Memphis and is 45 years old now, I have one grand daughter she lives in Oregon and she's almost 40 but that's the extent of it all of my brothers and sisters have gone on ahead of me.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your view of the military at all?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Yes sure did I don't know how to tell you what is there anything specific about that you need to ask I'm patriotic and wouldn't really want to get into this war now o yes it was a good impression, well I back in World War II everyone wanted to be in the military like Vietnam that was not a popular situation like Korea all of these or the situation were in right now, but I you know since I served in two wars I feel like some of these people that don't even wanna be in the service and slander our presidents and all I don't go along with all of that I'm patriotic, I don't have flag flying out front because someone stole it.

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: How did your military experience effect your life in the long run?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: For one thing it taught me how to make up a bed clean house cook in a small way well now the military didn't teach me how to cook taught me to respect my elders taught me a lot I think its good for all young men to have some service of some kind its bad right now with all over in Korea it shaped my life a lot

sp.speaker: James Arena
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Frank D. Buehl
sp.p: Well.... Like I said I was in the lumber business for 40 years did a lot of traveling, my business was in Memphis and I did most of my business in California. People don't understand that because there's so many trees and lumber produced out there that comes here but they don't have the type of lumber out there that we have here like hardwoods like that oak tree out there they don't have trees like and many species, I did a lot of traveling during my career mainly out west. And now a day I don't like traveling to much of a hassle to get on an airplane and go any place. Now you ask me about things in general, I played golf all of my life I think I started when I was 8 I play golf about 2 times a week with some of my friends who are retired, like yesterday was a golf day but it rained, and tomorrow is a golf day and it gives me something to do it keeps me busy except I do like to work in the yard but I cant do much of that, or in the months ahead, so I, I do have a heart problem last year I had surgery on my heart about a month before my wife died so that wasn't a good time but I still go to a cardiologist on a regular basis, I wear a pace maker for my heart, but why am I talking about this now you asked me to do something didn't you, I don't wanna tell you about my personal problems and things like that, the most memorable things happened in Greece that I told you about earlier but I didn't elaborate into it but that's a copy of a congressional record up there, which somehow my story got out and it ended up there, those are photos of my friend and some of my crew up there, you running out of? Alright lets see I'm not.

Pictures. That's a b-24 two heavy bombers b-17 and b-24. Heres an interesting photo right here if you can see it that's in Greece in the middle of the German occupation. These are Greek guerillas see these guys with these guns and all there are 11 of us with the Greeks, the Germans were in the valleys and we were in the mountains to evade the Germans, these are the people that took care of us for 19 days.

Here my this is my crew right here when they give you an airplane like that you put a name on it ours was Dirty Dirty, that was the co-pilot he was killed, navigator, bombardier he was killed, the engineer was captured bye the Germans he was wounded pretty badly. This is one of the gunners and was killed; the other was hit in the face and blinded. These 3 were captured by the Germans the reason was because they parachuted out of the plane too early and landed in a valley, me this one, this one, this one, all escaped. A German shell exploded in his face and made him blind.

These are some friends of mine in training that was in Greenville missippi These are my close friends he's passed away, he's alive and a little bit older this is another one of my good friends in training he's dead, so me and my other friend are the only 2 still left alive, I don't know what else I can show you.
That's my diploma, Febuary 1943. I don't know what else I can show you here.

0h yeah that's what Germans shot at us with that's a 20 mm explosive shell, this is the rip cord to my parachute and for some reason I held on to it, this is part of my parachute which the people in the occupied countries and treasured silk this Greek woman got a piece of the parachute and cut this portion hemmed it and gave it to me, this is another type of parachute material and this is not silk its nylon I believe. They used this for dropping supplies, these are Greek cigarette's.
*phone call*

...and I'll tell ya we lived in tents in the desert and sand got in everything and I know when I go on a mission when I went to fly I'd get my chute and stuff the silk in and dump sand out of it, that's part of my actual parachute. I don't know where I got that I really don't I don't know where it came from the powder and stuff is still in there, it's the little bag in the bottom there, its called a 20 mm explosive shell, I don't know a whole lot about munitions except this is the timing device up here and when it got time to go off it just exploded and slung this stuff everywhere, we called it flak.

This was from German planes, ME-109's and FW-190's. Those things can cause a lot of damage, but now is much bigger than that, yeah , ha , but I don't know what else I can tell you guys, when I came back from World War II plow incorporated they made medicine and they ran an article once a month about a returning soldier, I dontated money after that, that was in 1943 December 43.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
